entry.title: Turning food waste into a delicacy | From Labs to Lives

media:group.media:title: Turning food waste into a delicacy | From Labs to Lives
media:group.media:description:
How do almond hulls become vegan caviar? Through the power of federal funding.
Cody Yothers, co-founder of Optimized Foods in Davis, California, explains how his team uses the outer coverings of almonds to grow tiny, edible pearls of koji, a type of fungus. Those pearls take the place of fish eggs.
When the founders chose their first food, they wanted a challenge. Caviar has a taste and texture that are hard to copy. Yothers shares how decades of federally funded research at UC Davis gave his team a place to start and why the company still relies on that work to solve problems for its customers.
— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —
*SUPPORTING SUSTAINABLE FOOD* Learn the three ways public research supports a more sustainable food industry and how it shaped the journey of Optimized Foods. https://www.ucdavis.edu/research/labs-to-lives/blog/sustainable-food?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=labs-to-lives
*HOW RESEARCH MAKES LIFE BETTER* This video is part of From Labs to Lives, a UC Davis series showing how research shapes everyday life. https://www.ucdavis.edu/research/labs-to-lives?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=labs-to-lives
— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —
*VISUAL DESCRIPTION* Small yellow spheres swirl in liquid. A wider view shows a clear tank in a lab, where two people in white coats stand beside the equipment. A gloved hand tips a flask filled with small beads. A man in a red shirt speaks on camera. Yellow text identifies him as “Cody Yothers, Co-founder, Optimized Foods.”
Harvesting machines cross a field, trailing dust. The Optimized Foods logo appears over a shot of people gathering leafy crops. A split screen shows almonds on one side and pieces of brown hulls on the other. A glass of orange pearls replaces the almonds. In the lab, a woman adjusts a microscope. Pale, ridged shapes fill a blue background, followed by a close-up of bright orange pearls.
In a kitchen, a gloved hand lets a crumbly mixture fall into a metal bowl. Back in the lab, Yothers talks with two people, and a hand tilts a flask of blue spheres. Glossy black pearls of vegan caviar fill a glass beside gold tins labeled “VEA.” A gloved hand scoops the caviar from an open tin. The next shots show it served over pasta and on small round crackers with a white spread and fresh dill.
A cook tosses round bites in a pan. A small jar is labeled “HYphat Sunflower.” Two people taste chocolates from a wooden board. Back in the lab, two people in white coats adjust a tall tank. The video ends with the UC Davis From Labs to Lives logo on a yellow background and the words “Learn more at ucdavis.edu/labs-to-lives.”

entry.title: Agrivoltaics: One Acre, Three Jobs | Unfold Podcast

media:group.media:title: Agrivoltaics: One Acre, Three Jobs | Unfold Podcast
media:group.media:description:
Solar panels and tomatoes may not seem like an obvious pair. At UC Davis though, they share the same field. Agrivoltaics is the practice of using solar panels in farm fields, creating energy while growing crops. Researchers say the solar panels have another job: saving farmers water by shielding crops from extreme heat. In this episode of Unfold, we step into a tomato field turned climate experiment to see what growers and scientists are weighing as the planet warms.
In this episode: • Majdi Abou Najm, UC Davis professor of soil biophysics • Gavin Chaboya, UC Davis Ph.D. student in Abou Najm’s lab • Kevin Logue, business development director at Sunlight Energy • Greg Roth, walnut farmer in Winters, California • Bruce Rominger, Yolo County farmer
Chapters 00:00 What is agrivoltaics? 04:12 Inside the UC Davis agrivoltaics test site 06:59 Can agrivoltaics save water? 9:51 Why aren’t more farmers using solar panels? 12:36 Can one acre grow food, save water and create energy?

entry.title: Preserving Research and Sustainability at UC Davis’ Living Laboratory | That May Be the Chancellor

media:group.media:title: Preserving Research and Sustainability at UC Davis’ Living Laboratory | That May Be the Chancellor
media:group.media:description:
In this episode, Chancellor May explores the UC Davis Arboretum, one of the campus’s outdoor treasures. He meets with staff, students, and researchers to discover how this 100-acre living laboratory connects hands-on learning, environmental stewardship and community engagement. From pollinator gardens to climate-ready oak groves, find out how the Arboretum serves as a hub for sustainability and innovation.
*Timestamps* 0:21 Introducing UC Davis’ living laboratory 1:00 Discussion of the GATEways Project and the Arboretum’s role in connecting human, animal and environmental health 2:14 Students share their hands-on experiences in the Learning by Leading program and Arboretum All-Starts garden 4:27 Chancellor May highlights the Living Landscape Adaptation Plan and campus resilience efforts to climate projections 6:21 Restored Arboretum Waterway and its impact on wildlife and research 8:46 Improving community and student health through 9:27 Commitment to accessibility, year-round community engagement and celebrating the Arboretum’s 90th anniversary
*About UC Davis Chancellor Gary S. May* Gary S. May became UC Davis’ seventh chancellor on Aug. 1, 2017. An accomplished scholar and engineer, May came to UC Davis from the Georgia Institute of Technology. More at: https://leadership.ucdavis.edu/chancellor/gary-s-may?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=chancellor_fltl

*About UC Davis* Since the beginning, we’ve outgrown expectations. Established in 1908 as a university farm, UC Davis has continually branched out, challenged the way things are done, and gained recognition for solving complex problems related to health, environment, culture and society. Our 5,300-acre campus borders the city of Davis, a vibrant college town of about 68,000 people in Yolo County.
UC Davis is among the most comprehensive campuses in the University of California system, with four colleges and six professional schools that offer over 100 undergraduate majors and more than 100 graduate and professional degrees. UC Davis enrolls about 40,000 students from over 110 countries and contributes at least $13 billion to the California economy each year. In the 2024-25 fiscal year, the university exceeded $1 billion in research funding for the third consecutive year, cementing its reputation as a tier one research university.

entry.title: UC Davis Researchers in the San Juan Islands

media:group.media:title: UC Davis Researchers in the San Juan Islands
media:group.media:description:
Experience the sights and sounds of the San Juan Islands off the coast of Washington for the capstone of the ecogeomorphology course, offered by the UC Davis Center for Watershed Sciences. This course has been offered for 24 years, spanning various rivers and coastlines from Alaska to Mexico.
UC Davis writer, Kat Kerlin, joined a class of 11 creative writers and scientists from campus and two outstanding guides as they sea kayaked from island to island, traversing 50 miles. By the end of the week, they discovered they had a lot to learn from each other, and from the surrounding nature.
Read more about Kat's journey through the seven islands: https://ucdav.is/4Bl87Nz
#UCDavis | #SanJuanIslands
Video description: Scenes from a sea kayaking trip ranging from paddling across open water, hiking through wooded areas and enjoying the shoreline.

media:group.media:title: Native American Heritage Month 2026
media:group.media:description:
Happy Native American Heritage Month! Join Chancellor May, Michelle Villegas-Frazier and Beth Rose Middleton Manning in celebrating the Native American community's heritage and contributions.
The UC Davis Native American Studies Department has been established for over 50 years and its graduate program for over 30 years. During this time, the department has made an international impact in terms of scholarships, services and alumni.
For more information about this month's events, visit https://ucdav.is/3JfSUau.
~UC Davis Land Acknowledgement~
We should take a moment to acknowledge the land on which we are gathered. For thousands of years, this land has been the home of Patwin people. Today, there are three federally recognized Patwin tribes: Cachil DeHe Band of Wintun Indians of the Colusa Indian Community, Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation, and Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation.
The Patwin people have remained committed to the stewardship of this land over many centuries. It has been cherished and protected, as elders have instructed the young through generations. We are honored and grateful to be here today on their traditional lands.
#NativeAmericanHeritageMonth
Video description: Chancellor May, Michelle Villegas-Frazier and Beth Rose Middleton Manning speak to the camera with a teal background with yellow text reading "Native American Heritage Month" and "UC Davis."
